title: Dreams versus Realities
primary_topics: Address at FLP's 10th Anniversary event, October 13, 2021 -- the 10-year mark since FLP's founding on October 13, 2011
The dreams-versus-realities framework: why slogans, tweets and theories fail to alleviate poverty, and why FLP's sustainable programs succeed
FLP's first decade (2011-2021): liberty programs -- Professorial Chairs, Legal Scholarships, Dissertation Writing Contests, Educational Assistance -- achieved and embedded
FLP's second decade (2021-2031): prosperity programs -- ESMEL fellowships for MBA students and the Entrepreneurship Fund of at least one billion pesos for MSMEs
sub_topics: Heaven-versus-hell joke: politician tours hell (grand palace, beautiful women, wine, lechons, lobsters, TikTok music, limousines, golf club, yacht, private jets) then heaven (immaculate white, harps, slow classical music, angels, no luxuries); chooses hell; finds waste, garbage, gnashing teeth; Devil: 'Yesterday we were campaigning and promising. Today you voted for us and chose our reality.'
Original version of joke: 'Yesterday, you were a tourist. Today, you are a resident'
Dreams-versus-realities theme: promise vs. fulfillment, theory vs. practice, tweets vs. substance, slogans vs. philosophies

The Marxist slogan challenge: 'From each according to his ability and to each according to his need' -- appealing to a dirt poor student but empirically disproven; China succeeded only after Deng Xiaoping's shift to entrepreneurship under One-Country-Two-Systems
CJP's acquaintance with Sison and Ocampo as student leader but his refusal to embrace communist slogans because he knew they could not be fulfilled in the real world
Bill of Rights negative language: 'No person shall be deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law' -- negatives not enough; positives needed
The Ten Commandments also mostly negative: 'Thou shall not kill'; 'Thou shall not steal'
Positive constitutional tenet: 'The goals of the national economy are a more equitable distribution of opportunities, income, and wealth...'
Two positive commands of Jesus: 'Love God with all your heart... and love your neighbor as I love you'
Election slogans: 'Alis diyan!' (Marcos vs. Macapagal); 'Tama na! Sobra na! Palitan na!' (Cory vs. Marcos) -- slogans rarely transform into substance

CJP's yearning: 1,200+ decisions mostly in negative language (commanding parties to stop illegal behavior, dismissing petitions); very few implementing positive provisions -- a 'throbbing yearning' that he had not done enough

FLP origin: organized October 13, 2011 -- 5 years after retirement, 16 years after entering the SC on October 10, 1995; invited by taipans and business leaders to join as independent director/adviser; learned of their CSR yearnings

FLP first decade: acquired 700-sqm condominium in Salcedo Village, Makati; Professorial Chairs, Legal Scholarships (20/year), Dissertation Writing Contests, Educational Assistance for the poor; scholars from all over PH -- U San Carlos, U Cebu, Ateneo de Davao, Ateneo de Cagayan, MSU, Fr. Saturnino Urios, U Cordilleras, St. Louis University
FLP Scholars Society: internal-binding mechanism while scholars pursue external propagation of the philosophy
Ultimate liberty project: Interactive Museum of Liberty and Prosperity in partnership with SC; mini-museum at Ayala Museum delayed by pandemic

FLP second decade: ESMEL fellowships (MBA with majors in economics, sustainability, business law, entrepreneurship); 'Entrepreneurship Fund' of at least P1 billion to invest in and help manage MSMEs with social impact but no bank access; Cezar Consing (former BPI president, Bankers Association of Philippines president) studying viability pro bono
Target date: celebrate FLP's 20th Anniversary in 2031; CJP will be 95 and 'hopes to still be around, healthy and happy, to join -- even in my wheelchair -- our celebration of triumph and fulfillment'

stances.claim: Slogans, tweets and theories fail as poverty-alleviation mechanisms because they are not backed by sustainable philosophies, implementable programs and realistic timelines. The hell-tourist joke is the definitive diagnostic: campaign promises look like luxury resorts; the reality of governance is garbage and gnashing teeth. FLP's answer is sustainable programs with no slogans.
stances.rhetorical_move: anti-slogan argument: the hell-tourist joke as the diagnostic tool for political promises; FLP's documented programs as the positive counter-model
stances.confidence: asserted with programmatic specificity (700-sqm office, 20 scholarships/year, specific regional universities)

stances.claim: The Philippine Bill of Rights, written largely in negative language ('no person shall be deprived...'), is necessary but insufficient -- the positive constitutional and legal provisions (economic goals, Jesus's two commandments of love) must be implemented to complete the constitutional promise. CJP's yearning in the Court was precisely this: most of his 1,200+ decisions commanded parties to stop illegal behavior rather than implementing positive provisions.
stances.rhetorical_move: negative-vs-positive constitutional argument: the Bill of Rights as an incomplete promise that FLP's programs are designed to fulfill

stances.claim: China succeeded economically not because of communist slogans but because of Deng Xiaoping's adoption of liberal democratic practice -- 'rewarding personal initiative and entrepreneurship while maintaining the communist system in their political governance.' The South Korea / North Korea comparison confirms the same principle: entrepreneurship, freedom and private initiative are the irreducible keys to prosperity.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-economics argument: two natural experiments (China + the two Koreas) as proof of the entrepreneurship-liberty-prosperity link

notable_anecdotes: The heaven-versus-hell joke: a corrupt politician tours hell (grand palace, Chickenjoy-like feast, TikTok music, golf, yacht, private jets), tours heaven (quiet, classical music, praying angels, no luxuries), chooses hell. When the door opens, it's hot, humid, ugly. The Devil: 'Yesterday we were campaigning and promising. Today you voted for us and chose our reality.' Original version: 'Yesterday you were a tourist. Today you are a resident.'

CJP's Marxist student temptation: as a dirt-poor student taking political science pre-law, his professor repeatedly challenged him to refute 'From each according to his ability and to each according to his need.' CJP could not easily negate it emotionally but knew the Soviet and Chinese realities. He did not become a communist, though as NUSP president he was 'well-acquainted with some of the young reds and pinks' of his time -- including Jose Maria Sison and Satur Ocampo.

The election slogan sequence: 'Alis diyan!' (Marcos against Macapagal), then 'Tama na! Sobra na! Palitan na!' (Cory against Marcos) -- slogans that worked politically but mostly did not transform into implementable substance.

CJP's throbbing yearning: despite writing the most decisions in the Court's history, 'there was a throbbing yearning in my heart that I have not done enough. Mostly, my decisions... were negative in language by commanding the parties to stop their illegal or irregular behavior.' The FLP is his positive-language institutional response.

The Cezar Consing pro bono study: former BPI president and Bankers Association of Philippines president is studying pro bono the viability and sustainability of the Entrepreneurship Fund -- acknowledging that the FLP needs financial-sector expertise to translate vision into bankable reality.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered October 13, 2021 -- the exact 10th anniversary of FLP's founding on October 13, 2011 (CJP's 75th birthday) -- this address opens with the heaven-versus-hell joke: a corrupt politician who chooses hell after being shown a campaign-promise paradise, only to find garbage and gnashing teeth on arrival. The Devil: 'Yesterday we were campaigning and promising. Today you voted for us and chose our reality.' The joke frames CJP's central thesis: slogans, promises, theories and tweets fail as poverty-alleviation tools because they are not backed by sustainable philosophies, implementable programs and realistic timelines. He traces his own near-Marxist moment as a dirt-poor political science student (acquainted with Sison and Ocampo) and his rejection of communist slogans despite their emotional appeal, citing Deng Xiaoping's One-Country-Two-Systems shift as proof that China's success came from entrepreneurship not ideology, and the South/North Korea contrast as the companion proof. He analyses the Bill of Rights' predominantly negative language ('no person shall be deprived...') as necessary but insufficient -- the positive constitutional economic goals and Jesus's two commands of love must also be implemented. He confesses a 'throbbing yearning' even after producing the most decisions in the Court's century-long history -- most were negative (stop the illegal behavior) rather than implementing positive provisions. He reports FLP's first decade: a 700-sqm Makati office, Professorial Chairs, 20 annual law scholarships (drawing scholars from Ateneo de Davao, Ateneo de Cagayan, MSU, Fr. Saturnino Urios, U Cordilleras, St. Louis, and others), dissertation writing contests, and educational assistance for the poor. He announces the second decade's centerpiece: ESMEL fellowships in MBA programs (economics, sustainability, business law, entrepreneurship) and the Entrepreneurship Fund of at least P1 billion to invest in and help manage MSMEs with social impact but no bank access -- with former BPI president Cezar Consing studying its viability pro bono. He closes hoping to be present at FLP's 20th anniversary in 2031, 'even in my wheelchair,' to celebrate 'triumph and fulfillment in the Lord's vineyard.'
